# HELD

> Measure on what you did not select.

HELD is a dependency-free tool that decides whether a claimed improvement in an
AI system or a robot policy is real. It measures the candidate against the
baseline on data that was never used to select the candidate, corrects the
selection-split gain for the winner's curse, and reports the verdict, the
uncertainty and the amount of held-out evidence the claim would require.

- Home: https://balanov.pro/held/
- Repository: https://github.com/Balanov/held
- License: MIT
- Language: Go, standard library only, one static binary, offline.

## Commands

- `held init` writes a starter measurement contract.
- `held check FILE` validates a contract and prints its SHA-256 pin.
- `held plan FILE` reports how many held-out items a declared gain needs.
- `held gate FILE --data FILE` decides whether the claim holds.
- `held render FILE` renders the protocol in English, Russian, Spanish and Chinese.
- `held seal FILE --data FILE` writes a pinned receipt.
- `held demo` writes the example scores.

Exit codes: `0` proven, `1` not proven or conflicting, `2` bad input.

## The contract format

One line of `key=value` clauses separated by commas. A value may be quoted and
may then contain commas; a semicolon separates list elements; a hash starts a
comment; newlines are whitespace.

    v=1, candidate=policy-v7, baseline=policy-v3, metric=success_rate,
    judge=state_check, selection=sel, heldout=hold, candidates=16,
    alpha=0.05, min_gain=0.01, power=0.8, locale=en;ru;es;zh

Keys: `v`, `candidate`, `baseline`, `metric`, `judge`, `selection`, `heldout`,
`candidates`, `corr`, `alpha`, `min_gain`, `power`, `locale`, `note`.

The canonical form is one line with a fixed clause order; its SHA-256 is the pin.

## The scores format

One record is one outcome of one system on one item, as JSON Lines or a JSON
array:

    {"split":"hold","system":"policy-v7","item":"h001","score":1}

`split` names the selection split and the held-out split, `system` names the
baseline and the candidate, `item` pairs the two systems, `score` is in [0,1].

## Why it exists

Self-improvement loops keep the candidate that scores best on a small evaluation
set and report that score. The number is inflated by the selection. Measured on
a synthetic benchmark with 2 000 rounds, 16 selection items and 16 candidates,
greedy acceptance wrongly keeps a candidate with no real improvement in 89.9 %
of rounds, a plain significance test on the selection set in 23.9 %, and the
held-out rule in 2.3 % against a nominal 5 %.

Published sources on the same failure: arXiv 2610.09239, arXiv 2607.25152,
arXiv 2609.31760, arXiv 2608.20290.

## Boundaries

HELD reads outcomes; it does not run models, agents or robots. It does not
explain why a candidate failed to improve, only that the improvement is not
established. The sample-size plan uses a normal approximation for a paired
difference. The benchmark is synthetic and reproduces the mechanism, not the
published numbers of any particular paper.
